docs.title: 1. Basics of Binary Search
docs.text:
Binary Search is an efficient searching algorithm used to find a target element in a sorted array. Instead of checking each element one by one, it repeatedly divides the search interval into two halves.

At each step, the algorithm compares the target value with the middle element:

  • If the middle element matches the target, the search is complete.
  • If the target is smaller than the middle element, continue searching in the left half.
  • If the target is greater than the middle element, continue searching in the right half.

This process continues until the target is found or the search interval becomes empty.

Important: Binary Search requires the elements to be sorted. For an ascending array, each comparison allows us to eliminate approximately half of the remaining search space.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Consider the sorted array:

[10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70]

Suppose we want to find the target value 60.

  1. The middle element is 40. Since 60 > 40, search the right half.
  2. The middle element of the remaining interval is 60. The target is found.

Instead of checking every element, Binary Search finds the target in just two comparisons in this example.

docs.title: 2. Sample Code (C++)
docs.text:
The following implementation uses an iterative approach to perform Binary Search on a sorted array.

#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

int binarySearch(const vector<int>& arr, int target) {
    int low = 0;
    int high = static_cast<int>(arr.size()) - 1;

    while (low <= high) {
        int mid = low + (high - low) / 2;

        if (arr[mid] == target) {
            return mid;
        } 
        else if (arr[mid] < target) {
            low = mid + 1;
        } 
        else {
            high = mid - 1;
        }
    }

    return -1;
}

int main() {
    vector<int> arr = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70};
    int target = 60;

    int result = binarySearch(arr, target);

    if (result != -1) {
        cout << "Element found at index: " << result << '\n';
    } 
    else {
        cout << "Element not found\n";
    }

    return 0;
}

Output:

Element found at index: 5

docs.title: Code Explanation
docs.text:
• low represents the first index of the current search interval.
  • high represents the last index of the current search interval.
  • mid calculates the middle index without adding low and high directly, helping avoid integer overflow.
  • If arr[mid] equals the target, the function returns its index.
  • If arr[mid] is smaller than the target, low moves to mid + 1.
  • If arr[mid] is greater than the target, high moves to mid - 1.
  • If the loop ends without finding the target, the function returns -1.

docs.title: 3. Time Complexity
docs.text:
Binary Search eliminates approximately half of the remaining search elements in every iteration. Therefore, the number of iterations grows logarithmically with the size of the array.

Case Time Complexity Explanation Best Case \(O(1)\) The target is the middle element in the first comparison. Average Case \(O(\log n)\) The search interval is repeatedly divided in half. Worst Case \(O(\log n)\) The algorithm continues until the target is found or the interval becomes empty.

Here, \(n\) represents the number of elements in the array.

For example, an array containing 1,024 elements requires at most about 11 comparisons in the worst case for this implementation.

docs.title: 4. Space Complexity
docs.text:
The iterative implementation uses a constant amount of additional memory. It only maintains a few variables, such as low, high, mid, and target.

Therefore, its auxiliary space complexity is \(O(1)\).

The algorithm does not create another array or use additional data structures proportional to the input size.

Note: A recursive implementation of Binary Search typically requires \(O(\log n)\) auxiliary space because of the function call stack.

docs.title: Four pillars of OOP
Definition:
docs.text: A interface is a contract that specifies what a class must do, without necessarily specifying how it does it.

docs.title: Some rules of interface:
docs.text:
• An interface is declared using the interface keyword.

  • An interface cannot be instantiated directly 

        Animal a = new Animal(); // Compilation error
    However, referece can be created : Animal a;

  • An interface does not have constructors: 

        interface Animal{
        Animal(){} // Compilation error
    }

  • An interface can contain :

    • Abstract methods
    • Default methods
    • Static methods
    • Private methods
    • Constants
    • Nested types (classes, interfaces, enums, and records)

  • Methods declared without a body in an interface are implicitly public abstract 

        interface Animal{
        void makeSound();
    }
    This is equivalent to : 
    interface Animal{
    public abstract void makesound();
}

  • Abstract methods cannot have a method body 

    interface Animal{
    void makeSound(){
        Sysmtem.out.println("Sound"); // Compilation error
    }
}

  • A class implementing an interface must implement all its abstract methods, unless the class itself is abstract.

  • Methods implemented from an interface must be declared as public (because methods without body in interface are public by default. And sub-class cannot reduce visibility of super-class). 

        class Dog implements Animal {
    @Override
        public void makeSound() {
                System.out.println("Woof!");
        }
    }

  • An interface can have private methods. They must have a body and can only be used inside interface.

  • All variables declared inside an interface are implicitly public static final.

  • An interface can extend one or multiple interfaces using extends.

  • A class uses implements to implement an interface. 

        class Dog implements Animal{}

  • A class can implement multiple interfaces. 

        class Machine implements Printable, Scannable { }

docs.title: More about four pillars
OOP Fundamentals
docs.text:
What is OOP?

OOP is a programming paradigm where programs are designed using objects that contain data and methods that operates on data. Its four main principes are encapsulation, abstraction, inheritence and polymorphism.

What is class?

A class is a blueprint or template that defines the data and methods that objects can have.

What is object

Object is an instance of class. It has its own state represented by its instance data and can use methods defined by its class.
